prose_1k@0.6.before:
Context compression is the practice of reducing the number of tokens an agent sends to a language model without discarding the information needed to complete the current task. A coding agent accumulates a large amount of material during a session: user requests, tool definitions, file reads, shell output, test failures, and its own previous reasoning. Most of that material is useful when it first arrives but becomes stale quickly. Left unmanaged, the prompt grows until it is expensive, slow, and eventually impossible to fit inside the model's window.

A typical coding agent spends most of its context budget on tool output. Build logs are especially wasteful because they repeat compiler banners, package manager warnings, and progress lines while only a few lines carry the actual error. Source files are dense and usually worth keeping intact. Prose from documentation sits somewhere in between: individual sentences are compressible, but removing the wrong clause can invert the meaning. A good policy therefore treats different content types differently instead of applying one global compression rate to the entire transcript.

There are two broad families of compression methods. Extractive methods select spans or tokens from the original text and keep them verbatim. Abstractive methods rewrite the text, which can achieve higher ratios but risks hallucinating details that were never present. Token-classification approaches sit in the middle: a small model scores each token as worth keeping or dropping, and the retained tokens are copied directly from the input. Because nothing is paraphrased, identifiers, file paths, and error messages survive unchanged whenever the classifier decides to keep them.
